analytic.title: SAQA: A Self-Adaptive QoS-Aware Scheduling Algorithm for Real-Time Tasks on Heterogeneous Clusters

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Nowadays, providing quality of service (QoS) guarantees for some applications such as signal data processing has become a critical issue. In this paper, we propose a novel s ¯elf-a ¯daptive Q ¯oS-a ¯ware scheduling algorithm called SAQA that sufficiently considers the adaptability for realtime tasks with QoS demands on heterogeneous clusters. When the system is in heavy load, the SAQA algorithm can degrade the QoS levels of new tasks or tasks waiting in local queues of nodes to guarantee high schedulability. The minimum QoS level is acceptable for each task. In contrast, when the system is in light load, SAQA can use slack time to adequately improve the QoS of new tasks. We compare SAQA with SAEDF algorithm by simulations. The experimental results indicate that SAQA has admirable adaptability while providing timing and QoS guarantees.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In large-scale computing, clusters have been considered as an attractive platform due to the outstanding costeffectiveness, excellent extensibility and usability. Nodes in a cluster usually with their own disks and operating systems are interconnected by high-speed networks, e.g. Myrinet or fast Ethernet, to provide high-speed processing of computationally large or data-intensive applications, such as weather forecasting [1], molecular modeling (computing the structures and properties of chemical compounds, biological macromolecules, polymers, and crystals) [2], etc. Specially, heterogeneous clusters receive a good deal of attention in practice because machines (nodes) with different processing powers are usually assembled in a cluster for economical purpose [3].

Nowadays, increasing attention has been drawn to develop and deploy real-time applications on heterogeneous clusters [3,4,5,6]. Real-time applications depend not only on results of computation, but also on time instants at which these results become available [5]. Generally, real-time applications are classified into two categories: soft real-time applications [6] and hard real-time applications [7]. As for hard real-time applications, catastrophic happens if some deadlines are missed, so all real-time tasks in the applications must be completed within specified deadlines. In contrast, missing few deadlines will not affect the soft real-time applications, but the real-time tasks should be accepted as many as possible [8]. Our study focuses on soft real-time applications.

It is noted that many of real-time applications have different quality of service (QoS) requirements including reliability, security, data accuracy and so on besides satisfying timing constraints. For example, real-time stock systems require high quality of security (a dimension of QoS) to guarantee the data processing on clusters not being read or altered by malicious users [9]. Authentication service, confidentiality service and integrity service can be supported to provide security for tasks and data [10]. In each service, multiple methods can be employed. For instances, SEAL, RC4, RC5, IDEA are all cryptographic algorithms for confidentiality but their security service qualities are different due to the different mechanisms used. And, higher security service quality is achieved at the cost of more processing time. Another example is that some signal data can be processed using different algorithms. As for decoding block turbo codes, several algorithms can be employed [11,12]. Note that, high-complexity algorithms can guarantee signal processing having higher QoS level (higher data accuracy) at the expense of processing time, but low-complexity algorithms are just the opposite. Therefore, developing a QoSaware infrastructure and scheduling algorithm on top of the structure are the keys for achieving efficient resource utilization, and improve the performance of real-time tasks on clusters.

Recently, there have been some efforts devoted to the problem of QoS-aware real-time scheduling. Unfortunately, to the best of our knowledge, most existing QoS-based real-time scheduling algorithms only strive to maximize the QoS level for each new task on the basis of satisfying timing constraints. These algorithms do not consider the adaptability, which is able to result in some tasks not being accepted when the system is in heavy load.

Motivated by the above argument, we propose in this paper a s ¯elf-a ¯daptive Q ¯oS-a ¯ware scheduling algorithm for soft real-time applications running on heterogeneous clusters, or SAQA, which is intended to consider the adaptability for QoS-aware real-time scheduling on heterogeneous clusters.

The contributions of this paper include: (1) A selfadaptive QoS-aware real-time scheduler model is given and analyzed. (2) An algorithm named SAQA is put forward based on the proposed scheduler model. ( 3) simulation methods and performance metrics are given to evaluate our approach. (4) Three groups of simulation experiments are carried out to test SAQA.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews the related work. In Section 3, we present a selfadaptive QoS-aware real-time scheduler model. Section 4 proposes the algorithm SAQA, and investigates its properties. Performance evaluation is presented in Section 5. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper with future work.

div.head: Related work
div.p: Scheduling algorithms for clusters have been extensively studied. Unfortunately, many practical instances of scheduling algorithms have been found to be NP-complete [13], i.e., it is believed that there is no optimal polynomialtime algorithm for them. These negative results motivated the need for heuristic approaches to develop scheduling algorithms.

Up to now, many heuristic scheduling algorithms have been proposed, e.g., Vallee et al. proposed a global scheduler which is able to dynamically change scheduling policies while applications are running on clusters [14]. Subramani et al. incorporated a buddy scheme for contiguous node allocation into a backfilling job scheduler for clusters [15]. However, they are not fit for real-time applications because of the lack of guarantee for real-time tasks to meet their deadlines.

The issue of real-time scheduling has been extensively studied based on heuristic in the literature, where various aspects of a complicated scheduling problem were addressed. Real-time scheduling algorithms can be either static (off-line) or dynamic (on-line) [3]. In static algorithms, the assignment of tasks to processors (nodes) and the time at which the tasks start execution are determined a priori [16]. Static algorithms are often used to schedule periodic tasks like that presented in literature [17]. However, those aperiodic tasks whose characteristics are not known a priori must employ dynamic scheduling algorithms, e.g., see [4,5,6]. Our work is focused on dynamically scheduling aperiodic tasks. In addition, several algorithms schedule tasks with precedence constraints, which are often represented by directed acyclic graphs (DAG) [3]. In contrast, we consider in this paper tasks having no precedence constraints because tasks with precedence constraints can be scheduled by transforming the precedence graph into independent nodes with new ready time and deadlines [18]. Moreover, some scheduling algorithms of real-time tasks are preemptive [19], whereas our scheduling algorithm is non-preemptive like that reported in [20], i.e., when a task starts to execute on a processor, no other tasks interrupt its execution, which is more efficient, particularly suitable for soft real-time applications than the preemptive approaches due to reducing the overheads needed for switching among tasks [21].

There exist some studies on QoS-aware scheduling for real-time tasks on clusters. Xie and Qin proposed an algorithm named SAEDF to schedule real-time tasks with security (a dimension of QoS) requirements [9]. Unfortunately, the SAEDF algorithm is a greedy one, it strives to maximize the QoS level of each new task based on satisfying its timing constraint, which maybe result in the schedulability of tasks being low. He et al. addressed a dynamic scheduling of parallel jobs with QoS demands and proposed a new scheduler TITAN that aims at improving performance measured by three metrics including over-deadline, makespan and idletime [22]. Although the TITAN considers some metrics, it is used in multiclusters or Grid environment. Abdelzaher et al. presented a novel scheme for QoS negotiation in real-time applications [23]. This scheme uses the batch mode, namely arriving tasks are collected and scheduled as a meta-task when a scheduling event is triggered. So, this QoS negotiation scheme focuses mainly on long-lived services that need to hold reserved resources for an extended period of time. In our algorithm, we exploit the immediate mode (schedule a task once it arrives). It is noted that these algorithms are all designed for homogeneous systems, making them unsuitable for heterogeneous clusters. And, they are lack of adaptability. As a result, we are motivated in this study to propose a novel scheduling algorithm to selfadaptively improve the QoS of real-time tasks running on heterogeneous clusters according to the system load.

In this paper, we propose a self-adaptive QoS-aware scheduling algorithm SAQA, which takes both the timing and QoS needs into account for real-time, independent, and aperiodic tasks on heterogeneous clusters. The SAQA algorithm is able to adjust the priority of scheduling objectives according to the system load. When the system is in heavy load, the high schedulability is the main goal. On the other hand, when the system is in light load, high QoS for accepted tasks is the major objective.

div.head: Scheduler model
div.p: The scheduler model can be categorized into distributed scheduler model and centralized scheduler model. In a distributed scheduler model, tasks arrive independently at each local scheduler, which produces schedules in parallel with other schedulers. In a centralized scheduler model, all tasks arrive at a central processor called global scheduler, from which they are distributed to nodes in a cluster for further execution. In this paper, we adopt the centralized sort. The reason is that the centralized scheduler model has two attractive features compared with the distributed scheme [3]. First, it directly provides the centralized scheduler with fault-tolerance using a backup scheduler. Second, implementation of a centralized scheduler model is simpler and easier than that of distributed scheduler model. Therefore, the centralized scheduler is employed in our scheduler model. In order to improve the scheduling quality, we add the feedback in the centralized scheduler.

Figure 1 shows the scheduler model. When a new task arrives, the global scheduler collects the information of tasks running on nodes and tasks waiting in local queues to calculate the earliest start time of the new task on each node, then the real-time controller and QoS controller in global scheduler will collaborate to decide whether the new task can be allocated or not, and what is the QoS level if the new task can be accepted. If the new task cannot be scheduled, it will be dropped into the rejected queue, otherwise it will be transferred to a destination node. After a new task is allocated to a node, the global scheduler will transfer the tasks' scheduling information to the node. The schedul-ing information includes execution sequences, selected QoS levels of the new task and tasks waiting in this node's local queue.

div.head: Task model with QoS requirements
div.p: In this paper, we consider a set T = {t 1 , t 2 , ..., t n } of independent real-time tasks with soft deadlines. And, each task has QoS requirements with several QoS levels specified by a user. The QoS in this paper refers to the data quality after processing. There is no communication among tasks while executing, and one task can only execute on one node. A heterogeneous cluster is composed of a set N = {n 1 , n 2 , ..., n m } of heterogeneous nodes with different processing powers. The execution time matrix is denoted as E = (e ij ) n×m , where element e ij is the expected execution time of task t i on node n j . It is assumed that the expected execution time is known. Techniques such as code profling/analytic benchmarking and statistical prediction have been devised to estimate e ij [?]. a i , d i , and f i represent the arrival time, deadline, and finish time of task t i , respectively. SAQA is a heuristic algorithm that combines the non-preemptive EDF (Earliest Deadline First) algorithm [21] and RF (Response First) algorithm [22]. When a new task arrives, the maximal quality admission test is performed. that is the task is given the maximal QoS level and is inserted into the local queue of a node by the deadline earliest first policy on condition that the task has earliest finish time on this node. If this test can guarantee the timing constraints of the new task and tasks whose execution sequences are later than that of the new task in the same node, allocate the task to the found node. Otherwise, degrade the QoS level of each QoS requirement by the Round-Robin policy untill it can be allocated. If the new task getting the minimal QoS level still cannot be allocated, select a node where the sum of QoS levels of tasks in its local queue is largest and then degrade these tasks' QoS levels using Round-Robin method. If all the levels of these tasks being degraded to minimal still miss the deadline of the new task or violate the timing constraints of tasks whose execution sequences are later than that of the new task, it is rejected, or it is allocated to the node.

div.head: Performance evaluation
div.p: In this section, we carry out three groups of simulation experiments to evaluate performance of the proposed scheduling algorithm SAQA. A competitive advantage of conducting simulation experiments is that performance evaluation on a large-scale cluster can be accomplished without additional hardware cost [9]. To reveal performance improvements gained by our proposed algorithm, we compare it with SAEDF algorithm proposed in the literature [9]. SAEDF sufficiently considers the goal of assigning highest possible QoS to incoming tasks but it ignores tasks that might arrive later, which is lack of the selfadaptivity.
In our experiments, to evaluate the performance of SAQA, we compare SAQA and SAEDF in the following metrics:
(1) Guarantee Ratio defined as: GR=Total number of tasks guaranteed to meet their deadlines / Total number of tasks × 100%;
(2) QoS Level Average used to test the QoS levels of accepted tasks;
From the comparisons with above two metrics , it is also easy to observe the self-adaptivity of SAQA.

div.head: Simulation method and parameters
div.p: (1) To present the node heterogeneity, we use p j a positive real number to represent the processing power of node n j . The powerAverage and powerSpan denote the average processing power of all nodes and variable scope taking powerAverage as center, respectively. p j is uniformly distributed between powerAverage -powerSpan and powerAverage + powerSpan. (2) We employ h i , a positive real number, to denote the hardness of task t i . The bigger the value of h i is, the longer the execution time of t i is. The execution time of tasks with bigger hardness is longer than that of tasks with smaller hardness on the same nodes. Parameters hardnessAverate and hardnessSpan denote the average hardness of all tasks and variable scope taking hardne -ssAverage as center, respectively. Similarly, the value hi is uniformly distributed between hardnessAverage-hardnessSpan and hardnessAverage + hardnessSpan.

(3) Because our scheduling model is a general one. So, without loss of generality, we only need to give an abstract QoS level definition. In addition, we just consider one group QoS requirement in our experiment, which is easy to be extended to multiple QoS requirements. As a result, we suppose that 0 ≤ q(x ij ) ≤ 9 is the current QoS level of t i on node n j , and q(x ij ) is a positive integer.

(4) The execution time matrix E = (e ij ) n×m can be classified into two classes: consistent and inconsistent. For a consistent matrix E, if node n x has a less execution time than node n y for task t k , then the same is true for any task t i . For a inconsistent matrix E, if processor n x has a less execution time than processor n y for task t k , then the same is not true for other task t i . In our study, the matrix E belongs to the consistent type. The execution time e ij of task t i on node n j can be generated as: e ij = (1 + q(x ij )/10) × baseT ime × (h i /p j ). Parameter baseT ime is a random positive real number.

(5) The deadline d i of task ti is chosen as follows: d i = a i +max{e ij }+baseDeadline [3]. baseDeadline is a random positive real number. baseDeadline determines that tasks have loose deadlines or not. (6) The arrival rate a i is described as: a i = a i-1 + intervalT ime. intervalT ime is a random positive real number.

div.head: Performance impact of node number
div.p: Figure 4(a) shows that SAQA always has higher guarantee ratio than SAEDF when the node number is less than 48. That is because when the system is in heavy load, schedulability is the main objective in SAQA. However, SAEDF selects the highest possible QoS level for every new accepted task with timing constraints, which will result in the new task having longer execution time, so the tasks arrive later have later start time. If the start time is delayed, the probability of missing their deadlines increases.

We observe from Figure 4(b) that the QoS level average of SAEDF is higher than that of SAQA when the node number is less than 48. That is because the SAEDF strives to maximize the QoS levels of all accepted tasks. But SAEDF gets higher QoS level at the cost of guarantee ratio. From Figures 4(a)-4(b), we also find that when the node number is 56, the guarantee ratio of SAQA is 100 percent and the QoS level average is higher than that of SAEDF. This can be explained that the system is in light load, so SAQA can guarantee higher QoS level for every accepted task.

Figure 4(a) and Figure 4(b) plot that when the node number is smaller resulting in the system is in heavy load, SAQA can guarantee higher guarantee ratio than SAEDF by degrading the QoS levels within an accepted QoS scope. In contrast, when the node number increases, the system is in light load, SAQA provides higher QoS level while guaranteeing higher guarantee ratio. This experimental results indicate that SAQA is with significant adaptivity. so some tasks arriving later have later start time and miss their deadlines. With the increase of intervalT ime, the number of tasks waiting in local queues decreases resulting in tasks have earlier start time. So, the guarantee ratio increases. Figure 5(a) also shows that SAQA has obviously higher guarantee ratio than SAEDF when intervalT ime is less than 2.1. That is because SAQA degrades the QoS levels of tasks waiting in local queues to decrease the total execution time of these tasks, so more tasks can be accepted for earlier start time.

div.head: Performance impact of arrival rate
div.p: Figure 5(b) shows that when the intervalT ime is increased from 0.5 to 2.0, SAEDF performs better than SAQA in QoS level average. That is because the SAEDF is only in pursuit of higher QoS level of new arrival task, regardless of the tasks arriving later. On the contrary, SAQA adopts a self-adaptive scheduling policy striving to accept the new tasks by degrading the QoS levels of tasks waiting in the local queue of the same node if the new task misses its deadline using minimal QoS level. However, when the value of intervalT ime is more than 2.0, the condition is just the opposite, SAQA has higher QoS level average than SAEDF. This result can be explained that when tasks arrive slowly, SAQA does not need to accept a new task by degrading the QoS levels of tasks in the same local queue any more, and the QoS becomes a major objective. An interesting observation from Figure 5(b) is that when intervalT ime varies from 2.0 to 2.1, the QoS level average of both SAQA and SAEDF decrease suddenly. The reason is that the task heterogeneity resulting in some tasks (long tasks) have longer execution time, these tasks cannot be accepted until the value of intervalT ime is large enough.

The experimental results from Figure 5(a) and Figure 5(b) plot that when tasks arrive quickly leading to the system in heavy load, SAQA is able to accommodate more tasks than SAEDF. And, when tasks arrive slowly making the system in light load, SAQA can provide higher QoS levels to sufficiently utilize the system resource, which indicates the self-adaptivity of SAQA greatly outperforms that of SAEDF.

div.head: Performance impact of node heterogeneity
div.p: Figure 6(a) plots that SAQA basically keeps the same guarantee ratio with the increase of node heterogeneity. This result proves that SAQA is more suitable for heterogeneous clusters than SAEDF. From Figure 6(a), we can find that SAQA always has higher guarantee ratio than SAEDF although the node heterogeneity varies greatly. We attribute the improvement to the fact that SAQA considers the schedulability as its main goal when the node number is less or tasks arrive quickly.

Figure 6(b) shows that SAEDF has higher QoS level average than SAQA, but the improvements is not rational for real-time applications because the guarantee ratio is decreased observed from Figure 6(a). Figure 6(b) also reveals that the performance impact of node heterogeneity for both algorithms are smaller and the impact of SAQA is slighter than that of SAEDF.
Figure 6(a) and Figure 6(b) reveal the performance of SAQA keeps basically same regardless of node heterogeneity, which proves SAQA is a good self-adaptive algorithm.

div.head: Conclusions and future work
div.p: In this paper, we proposed a QoS-aware scheduling algorithm SAQA for real-time tasks on heterogeneous clusters, in which the adaptability for tasks with QoS demands is considered. In heavy load systems, the QoS level is de-graded to improve the schedulability. In light load systems, SAQA tries to maximize the QoS level of each task. Compared with the existing SAEDF that does not consider the adaptability to the system load, the experimental results show the improvements of SAQA in terms of the schedulability within heavy load systems and of the QoS level within light load systems. Adaptability to the system load with general QoS requirements is the novelty of SAQA. This flexibility provided by SAQA is useful for better utilization of heterogeneous cluster resources.
For future work, we will integrate multiple resources such as memory and network bandwidth into our model.
